questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The executive requires his assistant to run all sorts of ________ for him, including getting his laundry, picking up his children from school, and walking his dog.
questions.explanation: The collocation is run errands — short trips to do small jobs such as collecting laundry or picking up children.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q:
Alfred: "Her latest album feels completely derivative and uninspired."
Bruce: "________ It heavily relies on the out-of-fashion Euro-pop sound."
options: That's a bit of a stretch.
questions.explanation: Bruce goes on to criticise the album too, so he agrees: My thoughts exactly. The other three all express disagreement.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The law requires that this factory ________ the machines every week.
questions.explanation: After require that the verb is in the subjunctive (base form have), and the causative is have somebody do something, with no to.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: ________ a medic present at the scene of the accident, the victim would not have survived.
questions.explanation: A past unreal condition (would not have survived) needs an inverted past perfect: Had there not been a medic present = If there had not been a medic.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Sales figures released by the company are suspicious as they do not ________ shipment records.
questions.explanation: To square with something is to be consistent with it; the figures do not match the shipment records. Add up to means "total", live up to means "meet expectations".

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: His manuscript is ruined by a highly ________ style with barely coherent digressions.
questions.explanation: Discursive writing rambles from one topic to another — exactly what "barely coherent digressions" describes.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The famous movie star looks surprisingly casual today; his only ________ is a plain necklace.
questions.explanation: An adornment is something worn to add beauty, such as jewellery. Decoration and embellishment are not used for a piece of jewellery worn by a person.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: His explanation was so ________ that even the experts were unconvinced.
questions.explanation: Far-fetched = unlikely, hard to believe; hence nobody was convinced. Far-flung = distant, far-sighted = wise about the future, far-reaching = having wide effects.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Children are often described as ________, easily influenced by their parental and guardian figures.
questions.explanation: Malleable = easily shaped or influenced, which the sentence itself paraphrases.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Grace was praised for her ________ judgement when she reported the scammer pretending to be a police officer on the phone.
questions.explanation: Sound judgement = sensible, reliable judgement. A snap judgement is a hasty one and would not be praised.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Fans are excited at the prospect of a ________ between two beloved anime franchises.
questions.explanation: A crossover is a work in which characters from two different series meet.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: ________ a short self-paced online course, one can receive a certificate.
questions.explanation: By + V-ing expresses the means by which the certificate is obtained. Having completed is also grammatical, but by completing is the natural way to state the method, and the paper's intended answer.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Refrain from consuming cheese or cream if you are lactose ________.
questions.explanation: The fixed medical term is lactose intolerant — unable to digest lactose.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: For basing their argument on ________ evidence rather than verified documentation, the plaintiff's civil lawsuit was dismissed.
questions.explanation: Anecdotal evidence is based on personal stories rather than verified facts or documents — the contrast the sentence draws.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: If you ________ with the shares that you have, it might be your ticket to early retirement.
options: throw your hat in the ring
questions.explanation: Play your cards right = handle a situation skilfully to get the best result; here, managing your shares wisely.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Since the joke never ________ Ricky, we had to explain it to him, which was lame.
questions.explanation: The sense is that the joke was never understood: cotton on (to) = understand, "get" something. Square up to = confront, muscle in on = force one's way into, pander to = indulge.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: It took the panel quite some time to ________ this conclusion.
questions.explanation: Arrive at a conclusion is the collocation; reach takes no preposition, and jump to a conclusion means deciding too quickly, contradicting "quite some time".

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: ________ is comfortable with relocating the fragile fresco.
options: Both the restoration experts and the museum curator
The restoration experts as well as the museum curator
Either the museum curator or the restoration experts
Neither the restoration experts nor the museum curator
questions.explanation: With neither … nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the museum curator, so singular is fits. Both … and, as well as (agreeing with experts) and either … or the experts all need are.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Harry displays an ________ attitude to religion, often joking about heaven and hell.
questions.explanation: Irreverent = showing no respect for things usually taken seriously, such as religion.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: With no major releases ________, the media company decided to lay off a portion of its staff.
questions.explanation: In the offing = likely to happen soon. With nothing coming up, the company cut staff.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: ________, the movie was panned by critics as formulaic and lacking in substance.
options: Commercially successful though was the film
Successfully commercial though the film was
Commercially successful though the film was
Successfully commercial though was the film
questions.explanation: Concessive fronting: Adjective + though + subject + verb — "Commercially successful though the film was". No inversion of subject and verb, and the adverb commercially modifies successful.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Jerry's coach ________ for failing to defend his champion title.
questions.explanation: Write somebody off = decide that they are a failure or no longer worth attention.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Not until the files were declassified decades later ________ the true extent of the criminal operation.
questions.explanation: After a fronted Not until … clause the main clause is inverted with an auxiliary: did the public realize. The realizing happened after the declassification, so past simple, not past perfect.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: ________, I would have visited you a month ago.
options: Had it been for my fear of flying
Should I not be afraid of flying
Had I not been afraid of flying
Were it not for my fear of flying
questions.explanation: A past unreal result (would have visited … a month ago) needs an inverted past-perfect condition: Had I not been afraid of flying. Option A lacks not and would mean the opposite.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The journalist refused to disclose her source, even ________ legal action threats.
questions.explanation: In the face of = despite being confronted with (a threat or difficulty).

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: In preparation for a large incoming shipment, warehouse workers were instructed to ________.
questions.explanation: Clear the decks = remove what is not needed so as to be ready for something new — here, making room for the shipment.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Sabrina wrote down "baking soda for mom" on her shopping list, lest in her hurry she ________ it.
questions.explanation: Lest is followed by the subjunctive (base form) or should: lest she forget it.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The boy denied ________ the answer key, but his perfect score makes it hard to believe.
questions.explanation: Deny + V-ing: denied stealing. Having been stolen is passive and would make the boy the thing stolen.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The documentary was criticised not so much for what it said ________ for what it left unsaid.
questions.explanation: The structure is not so much X as Y.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Surrounded at Dien Bien Phu with their supply lifelines severed, the French forces were ________.
questions.explanation: On a hiding to nothing = in a situation where failure is certain and success impossible. In the doldrums = inactive or depressed; out on a limb = holding an unsupported position.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Realizing that his matcha-flavored dog food venture had completely failed, the entrepreneur chose to ________.
questions.explanation: Cut one's losses = abandon a failing venture before losing any more.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Only after the committee had reviewed the raw data ________ to publish the preliminary results.
questions.explanation: A fronted Only after … clause forces inversion in the main clause; the reviewing (past perfect) came before the agreeing (past simple): did it agree.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Growing up in a middle class suburban family, Alice is ________ from the hardships of inner-city children.
questions.explanation: Insulated from = protected from unpleasant experiences.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Nourished by rich silt, the Mekong Delta is a(n) ________ agricultural terrain.
questions.explanation: Fecund = fertile, producing many crops. Abundant describes quantity, not the productivity of land.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Lowering interest rates is often an economic ________ to encourage spending and investment.
questions.explanation: An economic stimulus is a measure to boost activity; stimulant is a drug, stimuli is plural.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q:
Molly: "________ our meeting to tomorrow afternoon?"
Holly: "________ Tomorrow afternoon actually works better for me."
options: Would you object to rescheduling / Yes, please!
Do you mind rescheduling / Of course!
Would you mind if I rescheduled / Not at all!
Would you be objected to reschedule / Never mind!
questions.explanation: Holly is happy to move the meeting, so the reply to Would you mind…? must be Not at all. "Yes, please" to would you object and "Of course" to do you mind would both mean she objects.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Passed down through generations, 'Quan Ho' singing requires vocal precision that is ________ to the region's identity.
questions.explanation: Intrinsic to = an essential, inherent part of. Ingrained takes in, not to.

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The university is offering grants in astrophysics, ________ have to be women currently pursuing a PhD program.
questions.explanation: Non-defining relative clause with a noun + of which: "grants, the recipients of which have to be women".

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Our dean announced extra funding for the faculty, only ________ it withdrawn two weeks later.
questions.explanation: only to + infinitive expresses a disappointing outcome; have it withdrawn is the causative/passive "have something done".

questions.part: Part 1. Language Use — Questions 1-40 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: I would rather you ________ the citations of your essay carefully before submitting it tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Would rather + subject + past simple for a present/future wish about someone else's action: I would rather you checked.

What makes people feel nervous about public speaking? Why do their hands shake, their knees quiver, their stomachs (41)____, and their voices rise?

Researchers find that public-speaking anxiety is both a trait (a general tendency) and a state (anxiety (42)____ by a specific audience or setting). Causes include fears of humiliation, failure, making mistakes, or being unprepared, alongside perfectionism and performance pressure.

Communication apprehension may have a biological basis; some individuals inherit a tendency to feel anxious. However, speakers can manage this by focusing on changeable behaviors, like enhancing speaking skills, rather than on their (43)____ makeup. Conversely, psychology affects biology. A speaker's perception of the assignment, skills, and self-esteem interact to create anxiety. (44)____ with conflict, the brain triggers a "fight-or-flight" (45)____, increasing breathing rates, adrenaline, and blood (46)____. These physiological changes cause a rapid heartbeat, shaking, quivering voice, or stomach "butterflies". (47)____, speakers may minimize eye contact, use vocalized pauses ("um," "ah"), or speak too rapidly. (48)____ uncomfortable, the body is simply attempting to assist with the task.

Regardless, apprehension seems to follow a predictable (49)____, with people generally feeling most nervous right before presenting, when uncertainty is highest. The second highest anxiety level occurs when the instructor explains the assignment, while the least anxiety is felt during preparation. Understanding this helps speakers manage anxiety when it (50)____. Because anxiety decreases once speaking begins and diminishes through positive preparation, starting early ensures both a better speech and greater confidence.
questions.explanation: A nervous stomach "flutters" (the "butterflies" mentioned later in the text); hands shake and knees quiver, but stomachs do not vibrate, shiver or murmur.

“Unless, of course, you tree huggers decide you’ll pay money to save it so you can enjoy it. Think your cronies can raise enough money to save the entire forest? (2)____

That one tree was a tiny part of a community of organisms thousands of years in the making. That community is made up of trees (“merchantable timber,” or “fiber,” in the jargon of the industry) that are a tiny minority of the lifeforms that comprise the forest.

(3)____

This is the community that we recognize as a forest, complex and interlinked beyond comprehension and all held together by the air, water, and sunlight that suffuse them.

(4)____

Consequently, companies require geneticists to breed fast-growing strains of commercially valuable trees, tree planters, herbicides to clear out “weed” (i.e., commercially worthless) species, insecticides to eliminate pests, fertilizers to restore nutrition to the soil, and firefighters. Large clear-cuts and the use of heavy machinery expose soil flora and fauna to sunlight, wind, and air. This alters water retention in the streams and rivers that are the lifeblood of the forest, radically transforming the remaining species mix.

(5)____

The entire forest is like the goose that laid golden eggs in the children’s fable; as long as the goose is fat and healthy, it will yield golden eggs indefinitely. In the short-term perspective of global economics, as in the children’s story, forestry companies attempt to gather all of the eggs at once by killing the goose.

(6)____

Returning to the CEO’s statement that the tree only acquires value when it enters our economy by generating revenue, consider what the tree does before humans define its value. Hundreds of years old, that tree has absorbed carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas) from the air, thereby playing a part in life’s climate engine, and releases oxygen as a byproduct of photosynthesis—not a bad byproduct for all animals like us that are completely dependent on that oxygen for survival.

(7)____

A. As I pointed out in the book Good News for a Change: Hope for a Troubled Planet, by selective logging at or below the growth rate of the trees in a forest, trees can be profitably “harvested” indefinitely instead of once every hundred years or more. Nor is the diversity that is the key to resilience and regeneration sacrificed when trees are selectively removed.

B. Recent studies on urban forestry indicate that compared to natural wild areas, isolated city parks do not offer the same microclimate stability. There, only invasive species and drought-tolerant shrub species thrive rather than native canopy trees. Because of this, urban planners cannot rely solely on localized tree-planting initiatives to emulate the effects of natural forests.

C. The soil is a living organism made up of tens of thousands of species of microorganisms—viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa—and larger nematodes, worms, insects, and mites. D. “You see that tree over there?” he shouted, pointing to a giant that was probably many centuries old. Without waiting for my response, he continued, “It doesn’t have any value until it’s cut down.” I was dumbstruck by the statement, giving him the opening to carry on.

E. Foresters rationalize these practices as “proper silvicultural management,” as if they know what it is that creates the original forest that was cut down. Of course, they have no idea. F. What had made me speechless was the realization that he was right. In the value system inherent in the form of economics our society has embraced, only when money is exchanged for goods and services is the transaction recognized as having economic worth.

G. Likewise, the roots of the tree cling to soil even under the hardest of rains, thereby inhibiting erosion while siphoning vast quantities of water up into the canopy, where it is released through transpiration, hence ameliorating weather. From roots to tips of branches, the tree offers a habitat for countless forms of life, from lichens and fungi to insects, birds, and mammals.

H. What foresters refer to as a “second-growth forest” is not a forest at all but a tree plantation—an attempt to grow trees like a crop of tomato or corn plants. But of course, such a “managed forest,” or “fiber farm,” no longer has the resilience, regenerative capacity, or self-protective devices of a natural forest.

I. Consequently, while carbon offset credits offer a lucrative alternative for developing nations to preserve forest areas, local enforcement often fails to prevent illegal logging operations along unmarked borders. This instability makes it difficult for conservation groups to project the long-term financial viability of these corporate partnerships.

British anthropologist Sir Edward Burnett Tylor espoused the classic definition of culture in 1871, describing it as that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, arts, morals, law, custom, and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society." Culture is learned; it is not something that is biologically determined. This is in contrast to our innate ability to acquire language. Regardless, the particular language an individual first learns – their "mother tongue" – can "only be acquired by man as a member of society." Language, therefore, is a part of one's culture, but at the same time, language is used to transmit that culture, to teach that culture. In fact, culture and language are interdependent. No type of human society can be maintained if its members do not share a common language. Moreover, language, the most common way people communicate, could not have developed outside a social setting.

Language both expresses culture and reflects culture. Some linguists and anthropologists argue that different languages produce different ways of thinking. Cultures organize and view the world in diverse ways, and their languages support these differences through grammar and vocabulary. By studying lexical classification in various languages, scientists have been able to show that speakers of different languages perceive and distinguish things differently. The Nuer people of Sudan, for instance, traditionally were cattle herders, and their entire lifestyle centered on cattle, so their language has dozens of words for cattle. Another cultural-dependent concept is time. English speakers divide time into past, present and future, and English grammar has tenses to reflect this view of time. On the other hand, the Hopi, a Native American tribe of the Southwest United States, only make a distinction between events that have existed or exist (English past and present) and those that do not exist or do not yet exist (English future, including the subjunctive case used for possibility). Their language does not differentiate between present and past. Similarly, the complexity of vocabulary in a language to describe family relationships varies depending on the role of kinship in that culture. Color terminology also varies widely by language. Those that involved in areas with a history of using dyes and artificial coloring have the broadest range of color vocabulary.

Living languages, of course, undergo constant but often gradual transformation, as new words and expressions are added to the lexicon and meanings of words are altered. Different cultures can speak the same basic language, but it will have variations reflecting those different cultures. For instance, Koreans share a common language, but after six decades of being separated by a tightly sealed border, the cultures of North and South Korea have diverged along with the Korean language. If a South Korean asks a North Korean how they are doing, the North Korean would likely reply "liupsopneda", an expression that literally means "not much," which has a sense similar to "I'm fine, thanks." Yet, that same expression would mean "Mind your own business!" to the South Korean. Both North and South Korean use the word "mije," but in the North it means "American imperialist," while in the South it means, "Made in the USA."

Within a culture, language can also play an important role in differentiating occupational groups and social status. Many groups have their own "focal vocabulary," that is, a specialized set of terms that are important to them and what they do. On a Hollywood film set, when the gaffer, head electrician, yells to the crew to "Kill the baby!" he is not talking about child murder. He is instructing the electricians to turn off a small light. Moreover, people want to improve their social status will try to adopt the habits, attitudes, and behavioural traits of the group to which they aspire. In terms of language, this includes trying to shift how they speak by taking on the speech patterns and vocabulary associated in their culture with the higher social status.

In any culture, language is more than just a means of conveying information. Significant aspects of a culture are embedded in the structure of its language, in its vocabulary, grammar, and usage. The distinctions a language makes between genders, how it refers to time and space, and the different ways language conveys rank, respect, and love are all related to the culture in which it is used.

British anthropologist Sir Edward Burnett Tylor espoused the classic definition of culture in 1871, describing it as that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, arts, morals, law, custom, and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society." Culture is learned; it is not something that is biologically determined. This is in contrast to our innate ability to acquire language. Regardless, the particular language an individual first learns – their "mother tongue" – can "only be acquired by man as a member of society." Language, therefore, is a part of one's culture, but at the same time, language is used to transmit that culture, to teach that culture. In fact, culture and language are interdependent. No type of human society can be maintained if its members do not share a common language. Moreover, language, the most common way people communicate, could not have developed outside a social setting.

Language both expresses culture and reflects culture. Some linguists and anthropologists argue that different languages produce different ways of thinking. Cultures organize and view the world in diverse ways, and their languages support these differences through grammar and vocabulary. By studying lexical classification in various languages, scientists have been able to show that speakers of different languages perceive and distinguish things differently. The Nuer people of Sudan, for instance, traditionally were cattle herders, and their entire lifestyle centered on cattle, so their language has dozens of words for cattle. Another cultural-dependent concept is time. English speakers divide time into past, present and future, and English grammar has tenses to reflect this view of time. On the other hand, the Hopi, a Native American tribe of the Southwest United States, only make a distinction between events that have existed or exist (English past and present) and those that do not exist or do not yet exist (English future, including the subjunctive case used for possibility). Their language does not differentiate between present and past. Similarly, the complexity of vocabulary in a language to describe family relationships varies depending on the role of kinship in that culture. Color terminology also varies widely by language. Those that involved in areas with a history of using dyes and artificial coloring have the broadest range of color vocabulary.

Living languages, of course, undergo constant but often gradual transformation, as new words and expressions are added to the lexicon and meanings of words are altered. Different cultures can speak the same basic language, but it will have variations reflecting those different cultures. For instance, Koreans share a common language, but after six decades of being separated by a tightly sealed border, the cultures of North and South Korea have diverged along with the Korean language. If a South Korean asks a North Korean how they are doing, the North Korean would likely reply "liupsopneda", an expression that literally means "not much," which has a sense similar to "I'm fine, thanks." Yet, that same expression would mean "Mind your own business!" to the South Korean. Both North and South Korean use the word "mije," but in the North it means "American imperialist," while in the South it means, "Made in the USA."

Within a culture, language can also play an important role in differentiating occupational groups and social status. Many groups have their own "focal vocabulary," that is, a specialized set of terms that are important to them and what they do. On a Hollywood film set, when the gaffer, head electrician, yells to the crew to "Kill the baby!" he is not talking about child murder. He is instructing the electricians to turn off a small light. Moreover, people want to improve their social status will try to adopt the habits, attitudes, and behavioural traits of the group to which they aspire. In terms of language, this includes trying to shift how they speak by taking on the speech patterns and vocabulary associated in their culture with the higher social status.

In any culture, language is more than just a means of conveying information. Significant aspects of a culture are embedded in the structure of its language, in its vocabulary, grammar, and usage. The distinctions a language makes between genders, how it refers to time and space, and the different ways language conveys rank, respect, and love are all related to the culture in which it is used.

Language and culture

Although humans possess the (1)____ to learn languages, they cannot effectively do so without belonging to a shared culture. In a similar fashion, cultures can hardly exist without a shared language between its members. This interdependence is demonstrated in multiple aspects. Firstly, vocabulary and grammar reflect the importance and perception of various domains in a culture. For example, cultures that highly regard (2)____ might have a richer vocabulary to denote relationships. Secondly, the (3)____ of any language constantly receives new additions as well as alterations to current words, a process which is tied to historical developments of the culture. Finally, within a society, language can be used to signify social group. This is illustrated by the (4)____ employed only in certain professions with very different meanings from their literal counterparts, while the words and (5)____ of desirable social groups are often copied by people who wish to be part of those groups.
